q: What does FAST stand for in stroke recognition?
a: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 112

q: How deep should chest compressions be in adult CPR?
a: 2 to 2.4 inches (5–6 cm) at a rate of 100–120 compressions per minute

q: What dose of aspirin is given in a suspected heart attack?
a: 325mg chewed (not swallowed whole) — only if conscious, not allergic, no contraindications

q: What is Beck's Triad in cardiac tamponade?
a: Low blood pressure, distended neck veins, and muffled/quiet heart sounds

q: At what BP reading is a hypertensive crisis defined?
a: Systolic >180 mmHg or diastolic >120 mmHg, especially with end-organ symptoms

q: What vagal manoeuvre can terminate SVT?
a: Valsalva manoeuvre — bear down hard for 10–15 seconds, or blow forcefully into a syringe

q: What is the "window period" for TPA use in ischaemic stroke?
a: Within 4.5 hours of symptom onset — time is critical, note exact onset time

q: What is the ratio of compressions to breaths in adult CPR?
a: 30 compressions : 2 rescue breaths. Hands-only CPR if untrained.

q: What is the Heimlich manoeuvre used for?
a: Relieving severe choking (airway obstruction) in adults and children over 1 year

q: What are signs of tension pneumothorax?
a: Absent breath sounds on one side, tracheal deviation, hypotension, distended neck veins

q: How do you manage a sucking chest wound?
a: 3-sided occlusive dressing (leave one side open as a flutter valve) — never seal all 4 sides

q: What is "silent chest" in asthma, and why is it dangerous?
a: No wheeze despite severe distress — means almost zero air movement. Imminent respiratory arrest.

q: Why must COPD patients NOT receive high-flow oxygen?
a: They rely on low O₂ to drive breathing — high flow can suppress their respiratory drive and cause apnoea

q: What does tripod position indicate?
a: Severe respiratory distress — patient leans forward on arms to use accessory muscles to breathe

q: When should you NOT remove an impaled object?
a: Never — stabilise it in place with bulky dressings. Removal can cause catastrophic haemorrhage.

q: When is a tourniquet indicated?
a: Limb bleeding not controlled by direct pressure. Apply 2–3 inches above wound. Note the time.

q: What is the recovery position used for?
a: Unconscious but breathing patients — keeps airway open and prevents aspiration

q: What is the difference between open and closed fractures?
a: Open (compound): bone pierces skin — high infection risk. Closed: skin intact. Both require immobilisation.

q: What are the signs of a base of skull fracture?
a: Battle's sign (bruising behind ears), raccoon eyes (periorbital bruising), CSF from nose or ears

q: What is the "golden hour" in trauma?
a: The first 60 minutes after major trauma when definitive surgical care gives the best chance of survival

q: How long should you cool a burn with water?
a: 20–30 minutes with cool (not cold, not iced) running water

q: What is the Parkland formula for burns?
a: 4ml × body weight (kg) × % BSA burned; give half in first 8 hours

q: What is the Rule of Nines for estimating burn surface area?
a: Head=9%, each arm=9%, chest=18%, back=18%, each leg=18%, perineum=1%

q: What burns should NOT be cooled with water?
a: Chemical burns (use dry decontamination first), electrical burns, and burns covering >20% BSA (hypothermia risk)

q: What are the signs of an airway burn?
a: Singed nasal hairs, hoarse voice, facial burns, sooty sputum — intubate early before airway swells shut

q: At what seizure duration should you call 112?
a: Any seizure lasting more than 5 minutes (status epilepticus)

q: What are the warning signs of meningitis?
a: Severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, fever, non-blanching rash (purpura)

q: What does a non-blanching rash indicate in a febrile patient?
a: Possible meningococcal septicaemia — call 112 immediately. Do NOT wait.

q: What is the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) and what score indicates coma?
a: GCS measures Eye (1–4), Verbal (1–5), Motor (1–6) responses. Score ≤8 indicates coma.

q: What is Cushing's triad, and what does it indicate?
a: Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular breathing — indicates dangerously raised intracranial pressure

q: What is the correct positioning for a suspected spinal injury patient?
a: Keep in-line neutral spinal immobilisation at all times — do not flex, extend, or rotate the spine

q: What is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis?
a: Epinephrine (EpiPen) 0.3mg IM into the outer thigh — NOT antihistamines

q: What should you do after giving an EpiPen for anaphylaxis?
a: Call 112 immediately — biphasic reaction can occur up to 12 hours later. Always go to hospital.

q: Where is the EpiPen injected and why?
a: Outer mid-thigh — large muscle with good blood supply for rapid absorption; can be given through clothing

q: What is a biphasic anaphylactic reaction?
a: A second wave of anaphylaxis occurring 1–12 hours after the initial reaction — reason all patients must go to hospital

q: What are the 4 systems involved in anaphylaxis?
a: Skin (hives/swelling), Respiratory (wheeze/stridor), Cardiovascular (low BP), GI (vomiting) — 2 or more = anaphylaxis

q: What are signs of severe dehydration in an adult?
a: Sunken eyes, no urination >8 hours, dry mouth, dizziness on standing, confusion

q: What is the oral rehydration solution (ORS) recipe?
a: 1 litre clean water + 6 teaspoons sugar + ½ teaspoon salt — WHO standard formula

q: What GI bleeding signs require immediate emergency care?
a: Vomiting bright red blood, black tarry stools (melaena), or large volumes of fresh blood per rectum

q: What are McBurney's point and Rovsing's sign?
a: Both indicate appendicitis — pain at right iliac fossa and pain there when pressing the left side respectively

q: What does RICE stand for for sprains?
a: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation — applied immediately to reduce swelling

q: What are the 5 Ps of compartment syndrome?
a: Pain (especially on passive stretch), Pressure, Paraesthesia, Pallor, Pulselessness — surgical emergency

q: How do you splint a fracture in the field?
a: Splint in the position found — immobilise the joint above and below the fracture. Do not attempt to realign.

q: What is the Ottawa Ankle Rule?
a: X-ray needed if pain at malleolus + unable to bear weight for 4 steps, or bony tenderness at posterior edges

q: What is the correct infant choking technique?
a: 5 back blows + 5 chest thrusts alternating — NEVER abdominal thrusts on infants under 1 year

q: What is the normal respiratory rate for a 1-year-old?
a: 24–40 breaths per minute. Fast breathing in a child is a serious warning sign.

q: At what temperature is a fever in a neonate (under 28 days) an emergency?
a: Any temp ≥38°C (100.4°F) in a neonate is a medical emergency — call 112 immediately

q: What is the "AVPU" scale?
a: Alert, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive — quick paediatric (and adult) consciousness assessment

q: What is the weight-based CPR compression depth for children?
a: At least one-third of the chest depth (about 2 inches / 5cm in children, 1.5 inches / 4cm in infants)

q: What are the stages of hypothermia?
a: Mild (32–35°C): shivering. Moderate (28–32°C): confusion, no shivering. Severe (<28°C): cardiac arrest risk.

q: What is heat stroke vs heat exhaustion?
a: Heat exhaustion: sweating, dizzy, normal mentation. Heat stroke: temp >40°C, altered consciousness — emergency.

q: How do you treat a jellyfish sting?
a: Remove tentacles with a card (not hands). Rinse with seawater (not fresh water). Soak in hot water 45°C for 20 min.

q: What is the first aid for a snake bite?
a: Immobilise the limb below heart level, apply pressure-immobilisation bandage, keep patient still, call 112. No cuts or sucking.

q: What is the antidote for opioid overdose?
a: Naloxone (Narcan) — given IM, IV, or intranasally. Repeat every 2–3 minutes if no response.

q: What is the SLUDGE toxidrome of organophosphate poisoning?
a: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defecation, GI distress, Emesis — treat with IV Atropine

q: Why should you never induce vomiting after caustic ingestion?
a: The corrosive burns on the way down AND on the way back up — doubling the oesophageal damage

q: What symptom triad suggests digoxin toxicity?
a: Nausea/vomiting + yellow-green visual halos + bradycardia. Antidote: Digibind (digoxin-specific antibodies)

q: What is the early warning sign of methanol poisoning?
a: Visual disturbances ("snowstorm vision") after apparent mild intoxication — blindness and death follow rapidly

q: What is the correct way to apply direct pressure to a bleeding wound?
a: Firm, continuous pressure with a clean cloth for at least 10 minutes — do not lift to check; it breaks the clot

q: When should a wound be left open rather than closed?
a: Bite wounds, highly contaminated wounds, and wounds over 6–8 hours old — high infection risk from closure

q: What is the correct wound irrigation technique?
a: High-pressure saline flush (at least 200ml) to remove debris — the solution to pollution is dilution

q: What are signs of wound infection?
a: Redness spreading beyond wound edges, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge, fever, and increasing pain after 48 hours

q: What is the difference between STEMI and NSTEMI?
a: STEMI: complete coronary blockage with ST-elevation on ECG — needs immediate PCI. NSTEMI: partial blockage, no ST elevation but troponin rises.

q: What is pulseless electrical activity (PEA)?
a: ECG shows organised rhythm but no pulse — causes include 5 Hs and 5 Ts (hypovolemia, hypoxia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, etc.)

q: What is Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome?
a: Accessory conduction pathway causing pre-excitation — can degenerate into life-threatening rapid arrhythmia; avoid AV-nodal blockers

q: What is the significance of a new left bundle branch block (LBBB)?
a: New LBBB with chest pain is treated as STEMI-equivalent — requires immediate cath lab activation

q: What is pericarditis and its classic ECG finding?
a: Inflammation of the pericardium; ECG shows saddle-shaped ST elevation in multiple leads and PR depression — treat with NSAIDs and rest

q: What is the difference between type 1 and type 2 respiratory failure?
a: Type 1: low O₂ (hypoxaemia) with normal/low CO₂. Type 2: low O₂ + high CO₂ (hypercapnia) — pump failure or COPD

q: What are the signs of an adequate bag-valve-mask seal?
a: Visible chest rise with each squeeze, no air leak sounds, and the bag refills completely between breaths

q: What is the first-line treatment for a tension pneumothorax?
a: Immediate needle decompression — 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line, before chest X-ray confirmation

q: What is Cheyne-Stokes breathing?
a: Cyclical crescendo-decrescendo breathing followed by apnoea — indicates brainstem compromise or severe cardiac failure

q: What SpO₂ level requires immediate supplemental oxygen?
a: SpO₂ below 94% in most adults; below 88% in COPD patients. Target 94–98% generally, 88–92% in COPD.

q: What is the ABCDE trauma primary survey?
a: Airway (with C-spine), Breathing, Circulation, Disability (neuro), Exposure — life threats treated as found, not after full assessment

q: What is the difference between haemothorax and pneumothorax?
a: Haemothorax: blood in pleural space — dull on percussion. Pneumothorax: air — hyper-resonant. Both: reduced breath sounds.

q: What is the golden hour in trauma?
a: The first 60 minutes after injury — definitive surgical control of bleeding within this window dramatically improves survival

q: What is a flail chest and why is it dangerous?
a: 3+ consecutive rib fractures in 2+ places — paradoxical chest movement. Underlying pulmonary contusion is the real danger.

q: What is damage control resuscitation?
a: Permissive hypotension (MAP ~50) + haemostatic resuscitation (plasma:platelets:RBC 1:1:1) + early surgery to control bleeding

q: What is the rule of nines for burns?
a: Head 9%, each arm 9%, chest 18%, back 18%, each leg 18%, perineum 1% — used to estimate total body surface area (TBSA) burned

q: How much IV fluid is given in the Parkland formula for burns?
a: 4ml × weight(kg) × %TBSA burned. Half in first 8 hours, other half over next 16 hours. Use Ringer's Lactate.

q: What burns should always be referred to a specialist burns unit?
a: Burns >10% TBSA, full-thickness burns, face/hands/genitalia/feet/joints, chemical/electrical/inhalation burns, or extremes of age

q: What is the first sign of inhalation injury?
a: Singed nasal hairs, soot in airway, hoarse voice, or stridor — intubate early before airway oedema makes it impossible

q: Why should you never use ice on a burn?
a: Ice causes vasoconstriction and can deepen the burn by extending tissue ischaemia — use cool running water for 20 minutes

q: What is the difference between a TIA and a stroke?
a: TIA: neurological deficit resolving within 24 hours (usually <1hr) with no infarct on imaging. Stroke: persistent deficit with tissue death. Both need emergency evaluation.

q: What is Cushing's triad and what does it indicate?
a: Hypertension + bradycardia + irregular respirations — indicates raised intracranial pressure and impending brainstem herniation

q: What is the GCS score and a score of 8 means what?
a: Glasgow Coma Scale (3–15): Eye + Verbal + Motor. Score ≤8 = severe TBI — protect the airway (intubate)

q: What is the difference between epidural and subdural haematoma?
a: Epidural: arterial bleed (lucid interval then rapid decline). Subdural: venous bleed (slower onset, often elderly/alcoholics)

q: What is postictal state?
a: Temporary confusion, fatigue, weakness after a seizure — lasts minutes to hours. If prolonged >30 min without waking, suspect status epilepticus.

q: What is the biphasic reaction in anaphylaxis?
a: A second allergic reaction occurring 1–72 hours after apparent resolution — reason all anaphylaxis patients need 4–6 hours hospital observation

q: Where is the correct site to inject an EpiPen?
a: Outer mid-thigh, at 90° angle — can be given through clothing. Hold for 10 seconds. Then massage site for 10 seconds.

q: What is the difference between allergy and intolerance?
a: Allergy: immune-mediated (IgE), can be life-threatening. Intolerance: non-immune (e.g., enzyme deficiency) — unpleasant but rarely dangerous.

q: Which antihistamine is preferred in anaphylaxis and why is it secondary?
a: IV chlorphenamine (Piriton) — it treats hives but does NOT reverse bronchospasm or hypotension. Adrenaline is always first.

q: What is the significance of latex allergy in surgery?
a: Cross-reactivity with banana, avocado, kiwi. Must use latex-free environment — even trace exposure can cause fatal anaphylaxis in sensitised patients.

q: What is Cullen's and Grey Turner's sign?
a: Cullen's: periumbilical bruising. Grey Turner's: flank bruising. Both indicate retroperitoneal haemorrhage — classic in severe pancreatitis.

q: What is the Blatchford score used for?
a: Predicts need for intervention in upper GI bleeding — factors include urea, haemoglobin, systolic BP, pulse, melaena, and syncope

q: What is paralytic ileus and what causes it?
a: Bowel stops moving without mechanical obstruction — causes: post-surgery, electrolyte imbalance (low K⁺), sepsis, opioids, peritonitis

q: What is Charcot's triad of cholangitis?
a: Right upper quadrant pain + fever/rigors + jaundice — indicates infected bile duct. Add hypotension + confusion = Reynolds pentad (septic shock)

q: What is the most common cause of acute pancreatitis in India?
a: Gallstones and alcohol abuse — GET SMASHED mnemonic for causes (Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion sting, Hyperlipidaemia/Hypercalcaemia, ERCP, Drugs)

q: What is the difference between a sprain and a strain?
a: Sprain: ligament injury (joint to joint). Strain: muscle or tendon injury (muscle to bone). Both graded I–III by severity.

q: What is a pathological fracture?
a: Fracture through abnormal bone (tumour, osteoporosis, infection) with minimal or no trauma — requires investigation of underlying cause

q: What are the Ottawa Knee Rules?
a: X-ray needed if: age >55, fibular head tenderness, isolated patella tenderness, inability to flex to 90°, or unable to weight-bear 4 steps

q: What is cauda equina syndrome and why is it urgent?
a: Compression of lumbar nerve roots causing saddle anaesthesia, bilateral leg weakness, and bladder/bowel dysfunction — surgical emergency within 24 hours

q: What is the appropriate management of a dislocated shoulder?
a: Do not attempt reduction without imaging and sedation. Immobilise in position found, give analgesia, urgent X-ray to confirm direction of dislocation.

q: What is the Paediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT)?
a: Appearance (TICLS: tone, interactiveness, consolability, look/gaze, speech/cry), Work of breathing, Circulation to skin — 30-second first impression

q: What is pyloric stenosis and its classic presentation?
a: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis in infants 2–8 weeks: projectile non-bilious vomiting after feeds, palpable "olive" mass, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis

q: What is the danger of a febrile convulsion?
a: Usually benign and self-limiting in children 6 months–5 years — danger is if it lasts >5 min (give diazepam), recurs, or has focal features

q: What are the Koplik's spots?
a: White spots on a red base inside the cheeks — pathognomonic of measles, appearing 1–2 days before the rash

q: What is intussusception and its classic presentation?
a: Telescoping bowel (usually ileocolic) in children 3 months–3 years — colicky abdominal pain, "redcurrant jelly" stools, palpable sausage mass

q: What is the dive reflex and how is it used medically?
a: Immersing face in ice-cold water stimulates the vagus nerve, slowing the heart — can terminate SVT in stable patients

q: What is the treatment for high-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE)?
a: Immediate descent, supplemental oxygen, dexamethasone 8mg loading dose — a portable hyperbaric chamber (Gamow bag) can be life-saving

q: What makes lightning injuries different from electrical injuries?
a: Lightning: massive DC current, brief exposure — causes cardiac arrest, keraunoparalysis, tympanic rupture. Safe to touch victim — no residual charge.

q: What is trench foot and how is it prevented?
a: Non-freezing cold injury from prolonged wet feet — causes nerve/tissue damage. Prevent by keeping feet dry and warm. Do not rub; rewarm gently.

q: What is the correct treatment for a dry chemical burn?
a: Brush off all dry chemical FIRST with a dry cloth before adding water — water activates some chemicals (e.g., quicklime) causing exothermic reaction

q: What is the toxidrome for anticholinergic poisoning?
a: "Mad as a hatter, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, hot as a hare, red as a beet" — tachycardia, dry skin, dilated pupils, hyperthermia, urinary retention

q: What is the antidote for organophosphate (OPC) poisoning?
a: High-dose IV Atropine (to dry secretions) + Pralidoxime (2-PAM) within 24 hours — common in India from agricultural pesticides

q: What is the antidote for benzodiazepine overdose?
a: Flumazenil — but use with caution; can precipitate severe seizures in chronic users or mixed overdoses. Supportive care is often safer.

q: What is activated charcoal and when should it be given?
a: Binds most toxins in the gut. Effective only within 1 hour of ingestion. Contraindicated for caustics, hydrocarbons, metals, and alcohols.

q: What is the classic presentation of carbon monoxide poisoning?
a: Headache, nausea, confusion in multiple people from the same enclosed space — "cherry-red" skin is a late sign. CO-Hb on co-oximetry confirms it.

q: What is the emergency treatment for chemical eye injury?
a: Irrigate immediately with copious saline or water for at least 20–30 minutes — do not delay for pH testing. Alkalis penetrate deeper than acids.

q: What are the signs of orbital cellulitis vs periorbital cellulitis?
a: Orbital: proptosis, restricted/painful eye movement, vision change — CNS extension risk. Periorbital: swelling confined to eyelid, eye moves freely.

q: What is sudden painless vision loss a sign of?
a: Central retinal artery occlusion ("eye stroke") — requires urgent ophthalmology, same workup as stroke. Window for treatment is 90–100 minutes.

q: What is a hyphaema?
a: Blood in the anterior chamber of the eye after blunt trauma — avoid NSAIDs (increase bleeding), keep head elevated 45°, eye shield

q: What are the danger signs in epistaxis (nosebleed) requiring hospital care?
a: Bleeding >20 minutes despite pressure, large volume loss, blood trickling down throat, on anticoagulants, hypertensive crisis, or post-nasal bleed

q: What is the ABCDE rule for melanoma?
a: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, Diameter >6mm, Evolution (change over time) — any one feature warrants urgent dermatology referral

q: What is necrotising fasciitis and why is it a surgical emergency?
a: Rapidly spreading deep tissue infection destroying fascia and skin — "flesh-eating bacteria". Pain disproportionate to appearance. Needs immediate surgical debridement.

q: What is the difference between urticaria and angioedema?
a: Urticaria: raised itchy wheals on the skin surface. Angioedema: deeper swelling of dermis/subcutaneous tissue — airway involvement is life-threatening.

q: What is impetigo and how is it managed?
a: Highly contagious superficial bacterial skin infection (Staph/Strep) — golden crusted lesions. Treated with topical mupirocin or oral flucloxacillin for widespread cases.

q: What is a keloid scar and how does it differ from hypertrophic scarring?
a: Keloid: grows beyond original wound boundaries, does not regress. Hypertrophic: stays within wound margins and can improve over time.

q: What is the difference between placenta praevia and placental abruption?
a: Praevia: painless bright red bleeding — placenta covers cervix. Abruption: painful dark bleeding with tender rigid uterus — placenta separates prematurely.

q: What are the warning signs of pre-eclampsia?
a: BP >140/90 after 20 weeks + proteinuria + headache, visual disturbances, epigastric pain, oedema — can progress to eclampsia (seizures)

q: What is the Apgar score?
a: Assessed at 1 and 5 minutes: Appearance (colour), Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration — 0–2 each, total 10. Score <7 needs intervention.

q: What is a cord prolapse and why is it critical?
a: Umbilical cord descends ahead of presenting part — compressed cord = foetal hypoxia. Position mother in knee-chest, push presenting part up, immediate C-section.

q: What is postpartum haemorrhage (PPH)?
a: Blood loss >500ml after vaginal delivery or >1000ml after C-section. 4 Ts: Tone (atony 80%), Tissue (retained), Trauma, Thrombin (coagulopathy)

q: What is the Safe Messaging approach when someone expresses suicidal ideation?
a: Listen without judgment, ask directly about suicidal plans, remove means if possible, stay with them, call iCall (9152987821) or take to emergency

q: What is serotonin syndrome and its triad?
a: Altered mental status + neuromuscular abnormalities (clonus, hyperreflexia) + autonomic instability (hyperthermia, tachycardia) — caused by excess serotonergic activity

q: What is the difference between delirium and dementia?
a: Delirium: acute, fluctuating, reversible, often with a medical cause. Dementia: gradual, progressive, chronic — but delirium can be superimposed on dementia

q: What is a panic attack vs a cardiac event differentiation challenge?
a: Symptoms overlap (chest pain, palpitations, dyspnoea) — always rule out MI and PE first. Panic attacks typically peak in 10 minutes and resolve fully.

q: What is neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS)?
a: Life-threatening reaction to antipsychotics: hyperthermia, rigid muscles, altered consciousness, autonomic instability. Stop antipsychotic immediately, ICU admission.

q: What is the correct first aid for an avulsed (knocked-out) permanent tooth?
a: Hold by crown only, rinse gently, reimplant immediately OR store in milk / saliva. Do NOT store in water. Reimplant within 30 minutes for best prognosis.

q: What is Ludwig's angina?
a: Rapidly spreading cellulitis of the floor of the mouth — airway compromise risk. Requires urgent IV antibiotics and often surgical drainage/airway management.

q: What is dental abscess treatment in the field?
a: Analgesia (ibuprofen + paracetamol), warm salt water rinses, urgent dental referral. Antibiotics (amoxicillin) only if systemic signs or spreading cellulitis.

q: What is trismus and what does it indicate?
a: Inability to fully open the mouth (lockjaw) — can indicate peritonsillar abscess, tetanus, masseteric spasm, or TMJ dislocation — requires urgent assessment

q: How do you manage a dislocated jaw (TMJ dislocation)?
a: Patient unable to close mouth, jaw deviated. Reduction: thumbs on lower molars, downward then backward pressure with controlled force. Post-reduction soft diet.

q: What is the sepsis "1-hour bundle"?
a: Measure lactate, take blood cultures, give broad-spectrum antibiotics, start 30ml/kg IV crystalloid for hypotension/lactate ≥4 — every hour of delay increases mortality by ~7%

q: What is the clinical triad of meningitis?
a: Neck stiffness (meningism) + fever + photophobia — but absent in 50% of cases. Non-blanching rash = meningococcal septicaemia = immediate 112

q: What is dengue shock syndrome?
a: Platelet drop + plasma leakage causing haemoconcentration, hypotension — occurs during defervescence (when fever breaks). IV fluids are critical but must be carefully monitored.

q: What are the danger signs in malaria?
a: Cerebral malaria (confusion/coma), severe anaemia, blackwater fever (haemoglobinuria), respiratory distress, parasitaemia >5% — require IV artesunate in ICU

q: What is the window period for rabies post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP)?
a: PEP can be given at any time but is most effective if started immediately. Rabies is nearly 100% fatal once symptomatic — never delay after animal bite.

q: What is the Whipple's triad for hypoglycaemia?
a: Symptoms of low blood sugar + blood glucose <70mg/dL + relief of symptoms after glucose administration

q: What is Somogyi effect vs Dawn phenomenon?
a: Somogyi: rebound hyperglycaemia after nocturnal hypoglycaemia. Dawn: early morning hyperglycaemia from growth hormone/cortisol surge — managed differently

q: What is hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS)?
a: Glucose >600mg/dL, severe dehydration, high osmolality but NO significant ketosis — occurs in type 2 DM, often elderly. Mortality higher than DKA.

q: What is the 15-15 rule for mild hypoglycaemia?
a: Give 15g fast-acting carbs (3 glucose tablets / 150ml fruit juice), wait 15 minutes, recheck glucose. Repeat if still <70mg/dL. Follow with a snack.

q: What are the feet inspection criteria for diabetic patients?
a: Daily check for blisters, cuts, redness, warmth, or swelling — neuropathy masks pain. Any wound must be seen by a doctor within 24 hours due to infection and gangrene risk

q: What is the tetanus prophylaxis rule for wounds?
a: Clean wounds + <3 doses prior: give toxoid. Dirty wounds + <3 doses: give toxoid + immunoglobulin (TIG). Boosters every 10 years for all adults.

q: What is the difference between primary, secondary and tertiary wound closure?
a: Primary: closed immediately. Secondary: left open to heal by granulation (contaminated wounds). Tertiary (delayed primary): closed after 3–5 days once infection risk drops.

q: How should a bite wound be managed?
a: Thorough irrigation with saline under pressure, debridement, leave open (bites have high infection risk), antibiotics (co-amoxiclav), assess rabies/tetanus risk

q: What is a keloid risk factor and how does it affect wound management?
a: Dark skin, chest/shoulder/earlobe location, prior keloid — use tension-free closure, avoid unnecessary surgery, early silicone sheets post-healing

q: What is debridement and when is it needed?
a: Removal of dead/contaminated tissue from a wound — required for any wound with necrosis, eschar, foreign material, or signs of infection to allow healing

q: What is the toxidrome for sympathomimetic poisoning?
a: Tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, dilated pupils, sweating, agitation — caused by cocaine, amphetamines, pseudoephedrine

q: What is the antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose?
a: N-acetylcysteine (NAC) — most effective within 8 hours but beneficial up to 24 hours. Prevents hepatic necrosis by replenishing glutathione.

q: What is the antidote for iron overdose?
a: Desferrioxamine (deferoxamine) IV — chelates free iron. Gastric lavage and whole-bowel irrigation may also be used. Activated charcoal does NOT bind iron.

q: What is the specific antidote for digoxin toxicity?
a: Digoxin-specific antibody fragments (Digibind/DigiFab) — indicated for severe arrhythmia, hyperkalaemia >5.5, or ingestion of >10mg in adults

q: What is the "toxicology screen" limitation in clinical practice?
a: Standard urine screens miss many drugs (fentanyl, GHB, newer synthetics) — clinical toxidromes and history are more useful than waiting for lab results
